name: evmone
workload: Execution of five EVM contract benchmarks (erc20.approval-transfer, erc20.mint, erc20.transfer, snailtracer, ten-thousand-hashes) through the evm-bench runners.
claimed_speedup: evm-bench README table: sum of benchmark times evmone 66ms vs geth 235ms (README prints geth as 3.561x relative to evmone 1.000x); snailtracer 43ms vs 163ms; erc20.transfer 8.6ms vs 24.6ms; ten-thousand-hashes 2.4ms vs 13.2ms.
stars_or_usage: 979 stars; EVMC module usable as a geth plugin
tradeoffs: C++20 required. Exposes the EVMC API, uses intx for 256-bit arithmetic and ethash for Keccak. Two interpreters: Baseline (default, minimal JUMPDEST analysis) and Advanced (indirect call threading, expensive upfront bytecode analysis). Using it inside geth needs a geth build with EVMC support. ecrecover is implemented directly by evmone with degraded performance (README).
caveats: Evidence is the independent third-party evm-bench suite (ziyadedher/evm-bench, GPL-3.0, 225 stars, last commit 2024-03-19). Its README states no hardware, compiler flags or implementation versions, so the table is probably several versions old and not reproducible to tier A. How each runner is timed (process start, deployment overhead) was not inspected. evmone's own geth-vs-evmone HackMD report (notes.ethereum.org, blocked here) was seen only as a search snippet: geomean evmone/Baseline 784M gas/s vs Geth 161M gas/s. The repo CHANGELOG has only self-comparisons (v0.9.0: Baseline 26% faster than 0.8.0 and 18% faster than Advanced on a 4.0 GHz Intel Haswell with Clang 15). The ipsilon/evmone repo was formerly ethereum/evmone.
found_via: GitHub/WebSearch: 'evmone fast Ethereum Virtual Machine C++ interpreter benchmark faster than geth EVM', then 'evm-benchmarks github evmone vs geth vs revm'; opened ziyadedher/evm-bench README

name: WebAssembly Micro Runtime (WAMR) fast interpreter vs wasmtime Pulley
workload: CPU time per call on 17 shared interpreter-only cases (fib, sieve, crc32, matmul, convolution, audio DSP, call_indirect, xmrsplayer, vtable dispatch, graphql) with WAMR in fast-interp mode (AOT, JIT and Fast JIT off).
claimed_speedup: Geomean CPU time relative to the fastest runtime: WAMR 1.63 vs Pulley 2.09 on M4 Max E-cores (WAMR about 1.28x faster, derived from page data); WAMR 1.38 vs Pulley 1.68 on iPhone XS A12 E-cores (about 1.22x faster, derived from page data). Per case on M4: sieve 1.00 vs 1.38, crc32 1.00 vs 1.18, matmul_simd 1.00 vs 1.18, call_indirect 1.58 vs 2.70, xmrsplayer 1.72 vs 2.26. Pulley wins fib_tail (1.00 vs 1.68), relaxed_madd and sqlite3.
compiler_and_flags: WAMR main b70d708d (WAMR-2.4.1-364) plus 29 local patches, cmake Release, -O3 -mcpu=apple-a12, INTERP=1 FAST_INTERP=1 AOT=0 JIT=0 FAST_JIT=0 SIMD=1 RELAXED_SIMD=1 BULK_MEMORY=1 TAIL_CALL=1 REF_TYPES=1 EXCE_HANDLING=1, WAMR_DISABLE_HW_BOUND_CHECK=1; Apple clang 21.0.0 (Xcode 27.0); Pulley built with rustc nightly-2026-07-05, RUSTFLAGS="--cfg=pulley_tail_calls -C target-cpu=apple-a12", fat LTO, 1 CGU, wasmtime v49.0.0 plus 9 fork commits
hardware: MacBook Pro Apple M4 Max (12 P + 4 E cores), E-cores selected with taskpolicy -b, macOS 27.0; iPhone XS Max A12 Bionic E-cores, iOS 18.7.10
tradeoffs: Fast interpreter trades memory and code size for speed; the benchmarked build lacks GC, typed references, memory64, multi-memory and exnref. WAMR needs 29 patches (legacy exception handling, relaxed SIMD, PROT_NONE linear memory) for the Wasm 3.0 feature cases.
caveats: The benchmark repo (rebeckerspecialties/wasm-benchmark, 3 stars, MIT OR Apache-2.0, last commit 2026-09-26) is third party but its author maintains a patched wasmtime fork, and every runtime is restricted to pure-interpreter mode (no JIT/AOT) for App Store rules, so the baseline is wasmtime's Pulley interpreter, not Cranelift-native wasmtime. Numbers are relative CPU time per call (1.00 = fastest runtime on the case), geometric mean over 17 cases that every runtime runs, N=10. WAMR is benchmarked from a patched main snapshot with hardware bounds checks disabled (WAMR_DISABLE_HW_BOUND_CHECK=1) and compared with a Pulley fork carrying the author's table-mutability and call_indirect patches. wasm3 is faster than WAMR on most of the same cases (geomean 1.01 vs 1.63 on M4). Evidence for a known project (WAMR already catalogued); reported for the Pulley comparison.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'new WebAssembly runtime github ... benchmark vs wasmtime wasmer wasm3 WAMR coremark startup 2026' surfaced PR #6 of rebeckerspecialties/wasm-benchmark; opened its README and docs/runtime-comparison-2026-09-22.md

name: wasm3 vs wasmtime Pulley interpreter
workload: CPU time per call on the 17 shared interpreter-only cases of the wasm-benchmark harness; wasm3 v0.9.0 has no native tier.
claimed_speedup: Geomean CPU time relative to the fastest runtime: wasm3 1.01 vs Pulley 2.09 on M4 Max E-cores (wasm3 about 2.07x faster, derived from page data); wasm3 1.04 vs Pulley 1.68 on iPhone XS A12 E-cores (about 1.6x faster, derived from page data). Per case on M4: call_indirect 1.00 vs 2.70, xmrsplayer 1.00 vs 2.26, sieve.scalar 1.00 vs 2.85, audio_dsp 1.00 vs 2.35, fib 1.00 vs 1.13. The report states wasm3 is the fastest interpreter on nearly every case it runs.
compiler_and_flags: wasm3 v0.9.0 (0cd38327), no patches, -O3 -mcpu=apple-a12 -std=c99 -DNDEBUG -fno-exceptions, no WASI sources; Apple clang 21.0.0 (Xcode 27.0); Pulley built with rustc nightly-2026-07-05, RUSTFLAGS="--cfg=pulley_tail_calls -C target-cpu=apple-a12", fat LTO, 1 CGU, wasmtime v49.0.0 plus 9 fork commits
hardware: MacBook Pro Apple M4 Max (12 P + 4 E cores), E-cores selected with taskpolicy -b, macOS 27.0; iPhone XS Max A12 Bionic E-cores, iOS 18.7.10
tradeoffs: wasm3 supports only tail calls and extended-const among the Wasm 3.0 features tested, runs on only some of the cases (no SIMD, no exception handling, no GC), and the maintainer announced a minimal maintenance phase.
caveats: The benchmark repo (rebeckerspecialties/wasm-benchmark, 3 stars, MIT OR Apache-2.0, last commit 2026-09-26) is third party but its author maintains a patched wasmtime fork, and every runtime is restricted to pure-interpreter mode (no JIT/AOT) for App Store rules, so the baseline is wasmtime's Pulley interpreter, not Cranelift-native wasmtime. Numbers are relative CPU time per call (1.00 = fastest runtime on the case), geometric mean over 17 cases that every runtime runs, N=10. wasm3 runs only 21 of the 39 cases; the geomean covers the 17 cases that every runtime runs. Instantiation is its weak spot: the extended-const rows cost wasm3 62-122x Pulley's time. Evidence for a known project (wasm3 already catalogued); reported for the Pulley comparison, and wasm3 as measured is an interpreter-only result on Apple Silicon only.
found_via: GitHub: same wasm-benchmark repo as the WAMR entry (docs/runtime-comparison-2026-09-22.md)

name: UWVM2 (u2 interpreter)
workload: Wall time of 383 .wasm modules that both uwvm2's u2 interpreter and wasm3 could run, plus WASI algorithm kernels (ChaCha20, SHA512, BLAKE2s), on AArch64 Apple Silicon.
claimed_speedup: Wall-time ratio uwvm/wasm3 geomean 0.5957 over n=383 modules (u2 faster on average), median 0.7116; ChaCha20 398ms vs 515ms, SHA512 202ms vs 220ms, BLAKE2s 3094ms vs 3427ms (internal time).
hardware: AArch64 Apple M-series (exact chip not stated)
tradeoffs: Template-specialized opfuncs trade code size for speed (Mach-O __TEXT about 1.4 MB), so u2 is not a minimal wasm3-class interpreter. C++26 codebase. Tiered interpreter + JIT design; supports many platforms, WASI P1, and mmap or allocator-based linear memory.
caveats: First-party section 9.1 of the u2 interpreter README, labelled by the authors as 'not universal claims', from an AArch64/Apple Silicon workflow with no CPU model, compiler or flags stated. The 383-module corpus lives in /tmp/uwvm2test and is not published, and the cited analysis note test/uwvm2test/u2_vs_wasm3_asm_stitch_analysis.txt returned 404 on raw.githubusercontent.com. The README itself says memory-heavy and branch-heavy kernels can lose to wasm3. Not compared with wasmtime, wasmer or WAMR; wasm3 is the only baseline.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/wasm-runtime?l=c%2B%2B (only C++ repo listed), then raw README of runtime/compiler/uwvm_int

name: VMIR
workload: test/misc/src/sha1test.c over 64MB of random data, run as LLVM bitcode in the VMIR interpreter versus lli.
claimed_speedup: Core i7 3.2GHz: VMIR 4.8s vs LLVM LLI 7m39s (about 96x, derived from page data); native 0.39s. README: interpretation is about 10x slower than native.
hardware: Core i7 3.2GHz (exact model not stated); ARMv7 BCM2709 (Raspberry Pi 2): VMIR 1m42s, VMIR JIT 17.5s, native 3.54s
tradeoffs: Standalone C library that executes both LLVM bitcode (.bc) and WebAssembly (.wasm); the built-in libc is incomplete, no vector types, no C++ STL support, and the JIT exists only for 32-bit ARM and does not cover all instruction classes.
caveats: Single README table, one workload (SHA-1), no compiler or flags and no lli build configuration stated, so the 96x gap likely reflects lli being a deliberately unoptimised interpreter (the README says as much). The result is capped at tier C for that reason. lli is not a WebAssembly runtime baseline; VMIR is not compared with wasm3, WAMR or wasmtime. Last commit 2018.
found_via: GitHub: appcypher/awesome-wasm-runtimes C list; opened andoma/vmir README

name: EOS VM
workload: EOS Mechanics WASM CPU benchmarks run under the EOSIO blockchain, comparing EOS VM with the Binaryen and WABT engines EOSIO previously shipped.
claimed_speedup: Vendor claim (search snippet only): EOS VM runs the EOS Mechanics WASM CPU benchmarks up to 16x faster than Binaryen; WABT gave EOSIO 1.3 about 2x over Binaryen; EOS VM expected up to 6x more than that (up to 12x faster than EOSIO at launch).
stars_or_usage: used by Antelope (EOSIO) blockchains; 7 stars on the AntelopeIO repo
tradeoffs: Header-only C++ backend (except the softfloat library) with an interpreter, a JIT, bounded memory and watchdog-timer execution limits; built for deterministic, time-bounded blockchain contracts rather than raw peak speed. README says WAVM executes extremely fast but has unpredictable compile times.
caveats: The repo README has no numbers. The 16x/2x/6x claims come from EOSIO's Medium posts (EOS Virtual Machine blog and EOSIO 2 announcement), which are blocked here and were seen only as WebSearch snippets, so benchmark_url is null. An independent paper ('VM Matters', arXiv 2012.01032, snippet only) reportedly measured EOS VM at about 19,768ms on a matrix benchmark versus roughly 70ms for WAVM and wasmtime, so EOS VM is far slower than JIT/AOT engines and the win is only against the older interpreters Binaryen and WABT.
found_via: GitHub/WebSearch: 'eos-vm C++ header-only WebAssembly backend benchmark faster than wabt wavm' and 'EOS VM benchmark results compared to WABT Binaryen WAVM'; opened AntelopeIO/eos-vm README and commits page

name: RISVM
workload: examples/asm/primes.asm (prime sieve written in RISVM assembly) run on the VM versus equivalent programs in C++, Node, Lua and Python.
claimed_speedup: x86-64: RISVM 4.97s vs Lua 5.3 7.23s (about 1.45x faster, derived from page data) and Python 3.6.6 35.95s (about 7.2x faster, derived); C++ g++ 7.3 -O3 1.80s, node 8.10 2.18s.
compiler_and_flags: C++ row: G++ 7.3 -O3; RISVM build flags not stated
tradeoffs: About 1000 lines of C++ plus a Python 3 assembler; 16 registers, 70 instructions, no overflow or bounds checking, little-endian only. README says it is about 3x slower than native on x86-64 and up to 10x slower on Xtensa and AVR.
caveats: Toy-scale: a single microbenchmark hand-written in RISVM assembly versus idiomatic scripts, so it measures a low-level bytecode against high-level language VMs; versions (node 8.10, Python 3.6.6, Lua 5.3) are old and the machine is not named. Not compared with wasm3, WAMR or any wasm runtime.

name: Type-V
workload: Type-C programs compiled to Type-V bytecode versus equivalent node --jitless and python3 scripts: recursive fib(40), 100M-element array allocation and sum, nested member access in a large loop.
claimed_speedup: Mean execution time (bar charts in the README): array allocation + sum Type-V 0.828s vs node --jitless 0.892s (about 1.08x faster, derived from page data) and python3 1.307s; fib(40) Type-V 9.91s vs node 8.32s (slower) and python3 11.07s; member access test Type-V 0.689s vs node 0.494s (slower) and python3 1.164s.
compiler_and_flags: Python 3.12.3 (GCC 13.2.0), Node.js v18.19.1 with --jitless; Type-V build flags not stated
hardware: AMD EPYC (Family 25, Model 1) 2 logical processors at 2.4 GHz, 2GB RAM, Ubuntu 24.04.1
tradeoffs: Typed bytecode VM for the Type-C language (C11, minimal dependencies); no JIT, scavenger-only GC capped at 1MB allocations, not production ready, not documented or fully tested per its own notes.
caveats: Mixed result: the README says Type-V 'beats node on some benchmarks (unpublished)' but the published charts show it ahead of node --jitless only on the array test (by about 7%) and slower on fib(40) and member access. The numbers appear only in PNG charts that were read visually, and the baseline is V8 with the JIT disabled, i.e. only the Ignition interpreter. Kept as a flagged weak entry.

name: WAMR iwasm on the libsodium WebAssembly benchmarks
workload: 70 libsodium primitives (aead, hash, sign, box and others) compiled to WebAssembly, timed in each runtime, December 2022 results.
claimed_speedup: Geomean time ratio over 69 shared benchmarks (derived from page data): iwasm 0.683x of wasmtime (about 1.46x faster), 0.670x of wasmer-cranelift, 0.585x of node (V8); wasmer-llvm 0.872x of wasmtime for comparison.
tradeoffs: WAMR supports interpreter, AOT and JIT modes; AOT needs the separate wamrc compiler and build step.
caveats: Derived by the agent from the raw CSVs in jedisct1/webassembly-benchmarks 2022-12/res (libsodium benchmark times, lower is faster; native is 0.289x of wasmtime so lower = faster): geometric mean of per-benchmark time ratios over the 69 benchmarks present in both files. The repo carries no README, hardware, compiler or flag details (Frank Denis's blog posts with the methodology are blocked here), the runtime versions are from December 2022 (the repo was archived 2026-08-19), and the mode in which each runtime ran (for iwasm, interpreter vs wamrc AOT) is not stated in the repo. Evidence for a known project (WAMR already catalogued).
